specPoints.text: understand ionic bonding in terms of electrostatic attractions
understand why compounds with giant ionic lattices have high melting and boiling points
know that ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid, but do conduct electricity when molten and in aqueous solution

primer.text: From Ionic Bonding you already know how metal atoms hand electrons to non-metal atoms, leaving positive and negative ions. This note follows those ions into the solid they build: the forces that hold the structure together, why so much heat is needed to melt it, and why the same solid refuses to conduct until it is melted or dissolved.

lessons.title: Ionic bonding & giant ionic lattices
lessons.opening: An ionic solid is a tightly packed arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions, held in place by strong electrostatic forces that act in every direction. Those forces are the ionic bonds. Because the ions build a giant lattice with a fixed alternating pattern, melting the solid means overcoming attractions that run through the whole structure, which is why the melting points are high.
keyPoints: An ionic compound packs positive and negative ions alternately into a regular giant lattice.
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between opposite charges hold the lattice together in all directions.
High melting and boiling points follow, because the forces need a large amount of thermal energy to overcome.
The larger the charges on the ions, the stronger the forces and the higher the melting point.
Magnesium oxide, with 2+ and 2- ions, melts at a higher temperature than sodium chloride with its single charges.

low.restatement: Positive and negative ions stack in a regular pattern with strong attractions between every opposite pair. Those attractions grip the whole structure, so a lot of heat is needed to shake it apart, and doubly charged ions grip harder than singly charged ones.
low.analogy: Think of a wall built from alternating magnets: every magnet grips its neighbours on all sides, and pulling the wall apart means fighting every grip at once.
low.examPointer: When explaining a high melting point, name three things: the giant lattice, the strong electrostatic forces, and the large amount of energy needed to overcome them.

medium.restatement: The lattice owes its stability to electrostatic attraction acting between every oppositely charged pair, in every direction, so no single link can be singled out as the one to break. Melting or boiling requires enough thermal energy to loosen the entire array, and the ion charge magnitudes set the force strength, which is why magnesium oxide outranks sodium chloride.
medium.analogy: Picture a velcro sheet where every hook catches every loop it meets: the bigger the hooks, the tighter the sheet, and separating it means peeling the whole surface at once.
medium.examPointer: Comparison questions expect the charge link made explicit: state that a 2+/2- pair attracts more strongly than a 1+/1- pair, then attach the consequence to the melting point order.

check.stem: What holds an ionic compound together?

options.text: Electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions, acting in all directions
options.explanation: The attractions run between every oppositely charged pair throughout the lattice, not along one line.

options.text: Covalent bonds between the ions' outer shells
options.explanation: The ions are already charged particles; sharing electron pairs belongs to covalent bonding between atoms.

options.text: Gravity between the heavy ions
options.explanation: Electrostatic attraction vastly outweighs gravitational effects at atomic scale; charges, not masses, do the gripping.

options.text: A sea of delocalised electrons around the ions
options.explanation: Delocalised electrons belong to metallic bonding; an ionic solid has no free electrons between its ions.

check.stem: Why does magnesium oxide have a higher melting point than sodium chloride?

options.text: Its ions carry 2+ and 2- charges, so the electrostatic forces are stronger and need more energy to overcome
options.explanation: Force strength rises with charge size, and magnesium oxide's doubly charged ions attract more strongly than sodium chloride's singly charged pair.

options.text: Its ions are heavier
options.explanation: Melting depends on the strength of the attractions, not on the mass of the ions.

options.text: Its lattice contains fewer ions
options.explanation: Both compounds form giant lattices; ion counts per unit do not explain the melting order.

options.text: Oxygen ions are smaller than chloride ions
options.explanation: The decisive difference is the size of the charges; ion radius is not the factor the explanation turns on.

check.stem: Which statement about the forces in an ionic lattice is correct?

options.text: They act between oppositely charged ions in every direction throughout the structure
options.explanation: Each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge on all sides, so the attractions fill the whole lattice.

options.text: They act only between nearest-neighbour rows
options.explanation: The forces are not confined to rows or planes; every opposite pair in reach attracts.

options.text: They act only while the solid stays cold
options.explanation: The attractions persist until melting; heat supplies energy against them rather than switching them off.

options.text: They are weak because many ionic compounds dissolve easily
options.explanation: The forces are strong; solubility depends on how water interacts with the ions, not on weak bonding.

check.stem: What must be supplied to melt an ionic solid, in terms of its structure?

options.text: Enough thermal energy to overcome the strong electrostatic forces across the giant lattice
options.explanation: Melting frees the ions from their fixed positions by paying the energy cost of the attractions.

options.text: Enough energy to break the covalent bonds inside each ion
options.explanation: No covalent bonds join the ions; even polyatomic ions keep their internal bonds intact on melting.

options.text: Enough energy to split the ions into atoms
options.explanation: The ions survive melting unchanged; only their positions become mobile.

options.text: Only a small amount of energy, because ionic lattices are fragile
options.explanation: The forces are strong and the energy demand is large, which is exactly why the melting points are high.
options.misconception: fragility confused with low melting point

check.stem: The ions in a lattice are described as alternating. What does that mean?

options.text: Each positive ion is surrounded by negative ions, and each negative ion by positive ones
options.explanation: Alternation places opposite charges side by side everywhere, which is what lets the attractions hold the structure.

options.text: The ions alternate between being positive and negative over time
options.explanation: Charges are fixed on each ion; only their positions are regular.

options.text: Positive and negative ions occupy separate layers
options.explanation: The pattern mixes the charges within the structure rather than segregating them into layers.

options.text: The ions alternate in size across the lattice
options.explanation: Alternation refers to charge signs; ion sizes follow the elements involved.
options.misconception: size pattern read as charge pattern

lessons.title: Conductivity of ionic compounds
lessons.opening: For a current to flow, freely moving charged particles must be present to carry it. In solid sodium chloride the ions are locked in their lattice positions, so the solid does not conduct. Melt the compound or dissolve it in water and the ions break free to move, which is why the molten liquid and the solution both conduct well.
keyPoints: Electrical conduction needs mobile charged particles, such as electrons or ions, to carry the current.
Solid ionic compounds are poor conductors because their ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move.
Molten ionic compounds conduct well, because melting frees the ions to travel through the liquid.
Aqueous ionic compounds also conduct, because dissolving in water releases the ions from the lattice.
It is the ions that move and carry the charge, never electrons, when an ionic compound conducts.

low.restatement: Ions locked in place cannot carry a current, so the solid does not conduct. Melting or dissolving unlocks them, and the mobile ions then carry the charge through the liquid, which is why the molten state and solutions both conduct.
low.analogy: Think of a car park where every car sits tightly in its bay: no traffic moves until the barriers open, and once released the cars can flow out in every direction.
low.examPointer: The classic trap is writing that electrons carry the charge in a salt solution; the moving particles are the ions, so name them explicitly in answers.

medium.restatement: Conduction demands mobile charge carriers. The lattice satisfies everything except mobility: the ions are charged but fixed. Melting or dissolving removes the positional constraint, letting ions migrate through the liquid under an applied field, so the molten compound and its aqueous solution both conduct, while the solid remains an insulator.
medium.analogy: Picture a flooded car park after the barriers fail: every car is free to drift with the water, and the crowd of moving cars is the current that the locked car park could never supply.
medium.examPointer: Contrast the three states explicitly when asked: solid non-conductor, molten conductor, solution conductor, and credit the freed ions as the carriers in the last two.

check.stem: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so no charged particles can move
options.explanation: The charges exist but cannot travel; mobility, not charge presence, is what the solid lacks.

options.text: Its ions carry no charge while solid
options.explanation: The ions keep their charges in every state; only their movement is restricted.
options.misconception: charge lost in the solid state

options.text: It has no electrons at all
options.explanation: Electrons are present inside the ions; they simply cannot move through the lattice to carry a current.

options.text: Its lattice reflects the current away
options.explanation: Conduction is about mobile carriers, not reflection; the solid simply lacks them.

check.stem: A beaker contains molten potassium bromide. Why does it conduct?

options.text: Melting has freed the potassium and bromide ions to move and carry the charge
options.explanation: The molten state releases the ions from their lattice positions, and the mobile ions are the current carriers.

options.text: Melting has freed electrons to move
options.explanation: The mobile particles are ions, not electrons, in an ionic liquid.

options.text: Molten compounds always conduct through their covalent bonds
options.explanation: Potassium bromide is ionic; its conduction rides on the freed ions, not on bonds.

options.text: The heat pushes ions from the anode to the cathode
options.explanation: The ions move in response to an applied electric field; heat alone only freed them.
options.misconception: heat mistaken for the driving field

check.stem: What changes when sodium chloride dissolves in water, compared with the solid?

options.text: The lattice breaks up and the ions move freely through the solution
options.explanation: Dissolving separates the ions from the lattice, so they can migrate and carry charge.

options.text: The ions gain extra charge from the water
options.explanation: Charges are unchanged by dissolving; only mobility improves.

options.text: Electrons flow through the water between the ions
options.explanation: The charge carriers in solution are the moving ions themselves.

options.text: The ions become molecules and stop carrying charge
options.explanation: The ions stay charged; that is precisely why the solution conducts.

check.stem: Which row correctly matches each state of an ionic compound to its conductivity?

options.text: Solid: does not conduct; molten: conducts; aqueous solution: conducts
options.explanation: Only states with mobile ions conduct, and both the melt and the solution have them.

options.text: Solid: conducts; molten: does not; aqueous solution: conducts
options.explanation: The solid has fixed ions and cannot conduct, while the molten state can.

options.text: Solid: does not conduct; molten: does not; aqueous solution: conducts
options.explanation: The melt frees the ions just as dissolving does, so it conducts too.

options.text: Solid: conducts; molten: conducts; aqueous solution: does not
options.explanation: The solution conducts through its dissolved ions, while the solid does not.

check.stem: In a conducting solution of copper(II) sulfate, which particles carry the current?

options.text: The Cu2+ and SO4 2- ions moving through the solution
options.explanation: The dissolved ions are mobile and charged, which is exactly what conduction requires.

options.text: Electrons travelling through the water
options.explanation: Electrons move along wires and electrodes; inside the solution the ions carry the current.
options.misconception: electron flow imagined through the liquid

options.text: Water molecules carrying the charge
options.explanation: Water molecules are neutral overall and are not the charge carriers here.

options.text: Copper atoms drifting between the electrodes
options.explanation: Copper atoms form only where ions gain electrons at an electrode; the solution carries ions, not atoms.
options.misconception: atom flow confused with ion flow

glossary.definition: Describing the forces of attraction or repulsion that act between electric charges.
The regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions in an ionic solid.
Describing a solid that has been heated past its melting point into a liquid.
Describing a substance dissolved in water.
A flow of charged particles, such as electrons or ions.

workedExample.prompt: a) Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. b) Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Explain both observations.
steps: a) Both compounds are giant ionic lattices held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, acting in all directions.
Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2- ions, whose doubly charged attractions are stronger than the 1+/1- attractions between Na+ and Cl- in sodium chloride.
The stronger the forces, the more thermal energy is needed to overcome them, so magnesium oxide melts at a higher temperature.
b) In the solid the ions sit in fixed positions in the lattice, so they cannot move and carry a charge — the solid does not conduct.
Melting frees the ions from the lattice, and it is the ions (not electrons) that move through the molten compound and carry the charge.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Mg2+/O2- attract more strongly than Na+/Cl-, so more energy is needed and MgO melts higher. b) Solid: ions fixed, no conduction; molten: freed ions move and carry the charge.
